summary:
Vichada stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Facilities and detention are governed by court order. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed, the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. More than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, The Guardian documented a 'social cleansing' campaign in which flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets; a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024, and discrimination limits trans women in Caquetá mainly to hairdressing or sex work. Vichada has no documented incident of its own in this material; the national finding carried to Vichada is that trans people are killed in daylight and on camera, and no arrest follows, alongside a pattern of territorial violence and displacement by armed actors.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's formal protections coexist with a decades-long civil conflict in which armed actors issue public kill lists and expulsion orders. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid that conflict. The UN Human Rights Committee has noted concern over the pattern of gender persecution.

Discrimination constrains economic life for trans women in several departments, where reported options narrow to hairdressing or sex work. This shapes what a trans visitor may observe in public space and who is visible on the street after dark.
